abstract: |
  Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 does more than replace Directive 2006/42/EC with a directly applicable machinery regulation. It extends the machinery-safety model into the digital mechanisms through which modern machines can be configured, connected, updated, remotely controlled, and intentionally manipulated. This article examines the Regulation's general legal changes and then focuses on its treatment of software, digital safety components, substantial modification, protection against corruption, malicious third-party attempts, communication-network failures, self-evolving behaviour, remote maintenance, and safety-related control systems. It distinguishes explicit legal requirements from engineering measures that may be used to satisfy them, analyses the role of functional-safety standards and IEC 62443, and places the Machinery Regulation alongside the Cyber Resilience Act, NIS2, and the AI Act. The central question is whether Regulation 2023/1230 changes the boundary of machinery safety itself: when software, connectivity, or external control authority can alter physical behaviour, protecting the integrity of the digital control system becomes part of preventing physical harm.

## The Machinery Regulation changes the boundary of machine safety

**Regulation (EU) 2023/1230** is not simply a recast of Directive 2006/42/EC. It preserves the classical machinery-safety model—risk assessment, inherently safe design, safeguards, safety-related control systems and information for use—but extends that model to the digital mechanisms through which machine behaviour can now be changed. The Commission itself describes the Regulation as integrating provisions for _cyber-safety_ concerning compliance-relevant software, data and safety control systems. The decisive legal provisions are Annex III §1.1.9, **Protection against corruption**, and §1.2.1, **Safety and reliability of control systems**. They require protection against intentional as well as accidental corruption and explicitly require control systems, where relevant to the circumstances and risks, to withstand reasonably foreseeable malicious attempts by third parties that could produce a hazardous situation. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-001]

That supports the central thesis of this research, but with an important boundary condition:

> **The Machinery Regulation does move machine safety toward cyber-physical safety, but it does not create a general-purpose OT cybersecurity regime. Cybersecurity becomes a machinery-safety requirement when compromise of a digital asset, communication path, software state, configuration or control authority can contribute to a hazardous physical state.**

Consequently, a vulnerability that exposes confidential production data may be important under the Cyber Resilience Act, NIS2 or company policy without necessarily violating a machinery essential health and safety requirement (EHSR)[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-ehsr-definition]. The same vulnerability becomes directly relevant to Regulation 2023/1230 if it enables an attacker to alter a safety parameter, inhibit a stop, trigger motion, defeat a protective function, corrupt safety-related data or otherwise cause a hazardous situation. That distinction follows from the safety-conditioned language of Annex III rather than from a generic requirement that every machine attain some undefined level of _cybersecurity_. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-002]

## The Directive becomes a Regulation: the legal baseline and the 2027 cut-over

Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 was adopted on 14 June 2023 and replaces Directive 2006/42/EC. Following a corrigendum concerning its dates of application, its main product requirements become mandatory on **20 January 2027**. Machinery first placed on the EU market before that date remains subject to Directive 2006/42/EC; the Commission expressly states that all machinery placed on the market before 20 January 2027 must comply with the Directive, although manufacturers may additionally state conformity with the Regulation where applicable. The Regulation is already in force as EU law, while different provisions on institutional machinery, delegated powers, notified bodies and penalties have phased in at different dates under Article 54. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-003]

The choice of a **Regulation rather than another Directive is substantive in institutional terms**. A Regulation applies directly and does not require each Member State to transpose its product rules into national legislation. The Commission identifies increased legal certainty through uniform application as one of the reasons and also notes alignment with the EU New Legislative Framework. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-004]

The basic product-safety architecture nevertheless remains familiar. The Regulation sets mandatory EHSRs; harmonised standards remain voluntary technical means for obtaining presumption of conformity where their references are published in the Official Journal. It also aligns machinery law more closely with the New Legislative Framework by formalising obligations across manufacturers, authorised representatives, importers and distributors and by integrating modern market-surveillance concepts. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-005]

### Scope and definitions

**Scope.** Article 2 covers machinery and what the Regulation calls related products: interchangeable equipment, safety components, lifting accessories, chains, ropes and webbing, and removable mechanical transmission devices; it separately regulates partly completed machinery. Important exclusions remain for, among other things, certain nuclear applications, weapons, specially designed military or police machinery, certain research equipment, mine winding gear, seagoing vessels and mobile offshore units, categories covered by vehicle legislation, and specified electrical/electronic equipment governed through other Union product regimes. The legal perimeter therefore still has to be determined product by product rather than by assuming that every automated industrial asset is _machinery_. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-006]

There are, however, several digital changes in the definitions themselves. The machinery definition expressly accommodates assemblies that are complete except for the upload of software intended for the manufacturer's specific application. More importantly, Article 3 makes a **safety component capable of being a physical or digital component, including software**, when it is independently placed on the market to fulfil a safety function and its failure or malfunction would endanger persons. Software can therefore be a regulated safety product rather than merely documentation accompanying hardware. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-007]

Partly completed machinery remains an assembly that is almost machinery but cannot itself perform the specific application and is intended for incorporation into or assembly with other machinery or equipment. Its manufacturer does not issue the same final machinery EU declaration of conformity; the relevant regime includes technical documentation, assembly instructions and an EU declaration of incorporation. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-008]

Defining the product perimeter, however, only establishes which regulatory regime applies. The next question is what conformity with that regime actually means. For machinery and related products, the substantive core is Annex III: the structured set of EHSRs against which the manufacturer's risk assessment, design measures, protective systems and technical evidence ultimately have to be justified. Understanding that structure is particularly important for the digital provisions, because the Regulation does not place _cybersecurity_ in a separate compliance silo; it embeds protection against digital corruption and malicious interference inside the machinery-safety requirements themselves.

### The EHSR architecture: how Annex III is organised

The EHSRs are the substantive safety requirements that machinery and related products must satisfy where they are applicable to the product and its hazards. Article 8 connects market access directly to them: machinery or a related product may be placed on the market or put into service only if it complies with the applicable EHSRs in Annex III when properly installed and maintained and used for its intended purpose or under reasonably foreseeable conditions.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-ehsr-article8]

Annex III is therefore not merely guidance and it is not itself a technical standard. It establishes the legally required **safety outcomes**. Harmonised standards can provide technical specifications and, where their references have been published for the Regulation and they cover the relevant requirement, a presumption of conformity; they do not replace the EHSR itself.

The structure is hierarchical. Annex III begins with definitions and general principles, then separates the requirements into a general set applicable across machinery and additional sets addressing particular categories or hazard classes.

| Annex III structure | Subject | Function in the conformity framework |
|---|---|---|
| **Part A — Definitions** | Terms used specifically for interpreting Annex III | Establishes the vocabulary through which the EHSRs are applied. |
| **Part B — General principles** | Risk assessment, applicability of requirements, state of the art and the relationship among the numbered sections | Establishes how the manufacturer determines which EHSRs apply and how risk reduction is to be approached. |
| **1 — Essential health and safety requirements** | General requirements for machinery and related products | Forms the principal horizontal safety framework. It includes safety integration, control systems, mechanical risks, guards, other hazards, maintenance and information. |
| **2 — Supplementary EHSRs for certain categories of machinery and related products** | Requirements for specific product categories, including food machinery, portable machinery and machinery for pesticide application | Supplements Section 1 where the machinery belongs to one of the specified categories. |
| **3 — Supplementary EHSRs to offset risks due to the mobility of machinery** | Mobile machinery, including control, movement, stability and autonomous mobile machinery | Adds requirements where mobility creates additional hazards. |
| **4 — Supplementary EHSRs to offset risks due to lifting operations** | Lifting machinery and lifting-related hazards | Adds requirements concerning stability, mechanical strength, load control and related safety issues. |
| **5 — Supplementary EHSRs for machinery intended for underground work** | Machinery intended for underground operation | Addresses the particular hazards of underground machinery. |
| **6 — Supplementary EHSRs for machinery presenting particular hazards due to the lifting of persons** | Machinery that lifts people | Adds requirements concerning carriers, controls, access and protection of lifted persons. |

: High-level structure of the essential health and safety requirements in Annex III of Regulation (EU) 2023/1230. {#tbl-ehsr-annex-iii-structure}

The Regulation consequently does **not** require every individual provision in Annex III to be applied indiscriminately to every machine. The manufacturer's risk assessment determines which requirements are applicable in light of the hazards presented by the machinery. The general principles also make clear that the requirements in the specialised Sections 2 to 6 supplement the general requirements of Section 1 rather than replacing them. Certain horizontal provisions—notably the principles of safety integration and specified marking and instruction requirements—apply irrespective of the conclusions of the individual hazard analysis.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-ehsr-general-principles]

For the cyber-physical analysis in this article, **Section 1 is the critical layer**. Its internal structure shows why the new digital requirements cannot sensibly be treated as an isolated cybersecurity appendix.

| Annex III provision | Subject | Relevance to cyber-physical safety |
|---|---|---|
| **1.1** | General remarks | Contains the general machinery-safety concepts on which the subsequent requirements depend. |
| **1.1.2** | Principles of safety integration | Establishes the risk-reduction hierarchy and the requirement to design machinery so that it can perform its functions without putting persons at risk under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse. |
| **1.1.9** | **Protection against corruption** | Introduces explicit requirements concerning connected devices, intentional or accidental corruption of hardware, software and data, identification of safety-relevant software, and evidence of intervention or modification. |
| **1.2** | Control systems | Establishes requirements governing the safety and behaviour of machine control systems. |
| **1.2.1** | **Safety and reliability of control systems** | Requires control systems, where appropriate to the circumstances and risks, to withstand relevant external influences, including reasonably foreseeable malicious attempts by third parties that could lead to a hazardous situation; it also contains requirements relevant to safety-function limits, software changes and self-evolving behaviour. |
| **1.2.2–1.2.5** | Control devices, starting, stopping and operating/control modes | Defines legitimate machine-control behaviour and authority—the behaviour that a successful cyber compromise may subvert. |
| **1.2.6** | Failure of power supply or communication network connection | Requires interruption, restoration or fluctuation of power or a communication-network connection not to lead to hazardous situations. |
| **1.3** | Protection against mechanical risks | Contains many of the physical hazard classes that corrupted software or control authority can ultimately activate. |
| **1.4** | Required characteristics of guards and protective devices | Relevant where digital manipulation can defeat, bypass or alter assumptions underlying protective systems. |
| **1.5** | Risks due to other causes | Covers additional hazard sources, including electricity, temperature, fire, radiation and other physical risks. |
| **1.6** | Maintenance | Governs safety considerations associated with adjustment, maintenance and intervention—the operational context in which privileged engineering access frequently occurs. |
| **1.7** | Information | Covers information and warnings on machinery, marking and instructions, including the Regulation's modernised treatment of digital documentation. |

: Section 1 of Annex III and the provisions most relevant to the transition from conventional machinery safety to cyber-physical safety. {#tbl-ehsr-section1-cyber-physical}

This structure is central to interpreting the Regulation correctly. **Protection against corruption in §1.1.9 and resistance to malicious influence in §1.2.1 are themselves EHSRs.** They do not sit outside the machinery-safety framework as a separate information-security obligation. A manufacturer assessing the safety of a connected control architecture therefore cannot first complete the _real_ machinery-safety analysis and then treat cybersecurity as an independent IT exercise. Where manipulation of a digital dependency can lead to a hazardous state, the digital dependency is part of the causal path addressed by Annex III.

At the same time, the structure prevents the opposite overinterpretation. Annex III does not transform every information-security weakness into a machinery non-conformity. The legal question remains tied to the relevant EHSR and ultimately to machinery health and safety. A confidentiality flaw in a production database, for example, is not transformed into a machinery-safety defect merely because the database is associated with the machine. If the same weakness allows an attacker to alter a safety configuration, issue an unsafe movement command or corrupt data on which a protective function relies, the connection to Annex III becomes materially different.

This distinction also explains the role of standards throughout the rest of the article. An EHSR expresses the **legally required outcome**; a harmonised standard may provide a recognised technical route to demonstrating conformity with part of that outcome; and engineering frameworks such as IEC 62443 may provide additional methods and controls for satisfying or evidencing security-dependent aspects of the safety case. These three layers should not be collapsed:

1. **EHSR → legally required safety outcome**,
2. **harmonised standard → technical specification** that may confer presumption of conformity within its cited scope,
3. **engineering control or framework → implementation mechanism** whose relevance must be justified against the hazard and requirement.

That hierarchy becomes especially important for §§1.1.9 and 1.2.1. Saying that a machine _uses IEC 62443_ does not itself demonstrate that the applicable EHSRs have been satisfied; conversely, the absence of an IEC 62443 certification does not by itself establish non-conformity. What matters is whether the manufacturer can connect the applicable Annex III requirement to the identified cyber-physical hazard, the chosen risk-reduction measure and the evidence that the resulting machine remains safe.

### Directive 2006/42/EC versus Regulation 2023/1230

With the EHSR architecture established, the comparison with Directive 2006/42/EC becomes more precise. Some changes concern the institutional and conformity-assessment framework; others alter the substantive safety requirements themselves. In particular, the explicit treatment of software, digital modification, intentional corruption, malicious interference and communication-network failure represents more than a reorganisation of Directive-era provisions.

The transition from the Directive can be summarised as follows.

| Topic | Directive 2006/42/EC | Regulation 2023/1230 | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legal instrument | Directive requiring national transposition. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-009] | Directly applicable Regulation; main application 20 January 2027. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-010] | **Structural change** |
| Economic operators | Manufacturer-centred model, with authorised representative and supply-chain duties distributed through EU product law. | Explicit NLF-style manufacturer, importer and distributor responsibilities, traceability and corrective-action duties. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-011] | **Clarification/modernisation with practical consequences** |
| Safety components | Predominantly understood through physical machinery components. | Definition explicitly includes **digital components, including software**. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-012] | **Substantive digital change** |
| Substantial modification | The Commission's Directive guidance treated sufficiently modified machinery as effectively new machinery, but the Directive lacked the Regulation's explicit horizontal definition. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-013] | Article 3(16) expressly covers modification by **physical or digital means**; Article 18 can make the modifier the manufacturer. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-014] | **Substantive legal clarification** |
| Cybersecurity | No equivalent horizontal requirement explicitly addressing intentional corruption or malicious third-party attacks. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-015] | Annex III §§1.1.9 and 1.2.1 explicitly address intentional corruption and reasonably foreseeable malicious attempts. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-016] | **Major substantive change** |
| Communication networks | Traditional electrical/control-system failure requirements. | Annex III §1.2.6 explicitly extends failure analysis to the **communication network connection**. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-017] | **Substantive digital extension** |
| Software traceability | Software faults were already relevant to control-system safety. | Explicit safe-software identification, intervention evidence and safety-software version tracing. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-018] | **Substantive change** |
| AI/adaptive behaviour | No dedicated self-evolving machinery framework. | Requirements for fully/partially self-evolving behaviour, ML-based safety functions and safety-decision records. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-019] | **Substantive change** |
| Remote/autonomous machinery | Remote-controlled mobile machinery was not wholly new as a concept. | Autonomous behaviour is addressed more systematically and now sits beneath horizontal digital-integrity/cyber-safety EHSRs. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-020] | **Mixed: continuity plus expansion** |
| Instructions | Predominantly paper-era model. | Digital instructions and declarations are expressly accommodated subject to conditions and availability safeguards. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-021] | **Modernisation** |
| Technical documentation | Conventional design/risk/test documentation. | Digital evidence becomes more important; Annex IV can require safety-related source code or programming logic to demonstrate conformity upon a reasoned authority request where other documentation is insufficient. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-022] | **Substantive compliance change** |
| Conformity assessment | Annex IV _high-risk_ categories under Directive procedures. | Annex I Part A/Part B structure; Part A mandates third-party routes and includes ML-based safety-function categories. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-023] | **Substantive reorganisation** |
| Market surveillance | Established machinery market-surveillance structure. | NLF-aligned duties, explicit economic-operator responsibilities and modern EU market-surveillance framework. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-024] | **Modernisation/strengthening** |

: Directive 2006/42/EC and Regulation (EU) 2023/1230: principal structural and substantive differences. {#tbl-directive-regulation-comparison}

### Conformity assessment and harmonised standards

The **conformity-assessment distinction in Annex I is particularly important**. Part A contains categories of machinery and related products for which a notified-body route is mandatory; it includes safety components with fully or partially self-evolving behaviour using machine-learning approaches that ensure safety functions, and machinery embedding such systems where the systems have not been independently placed on the market. Part B contains additional machinery categories for which internal production control remains available only under the Regulation's conditions concerning harmonised standards or common specifications; otherwise a notified-body route is required. Article 25 establishes the applicable procedures. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-025]

The Regulation does not abolish the harmonised-standard model. Article 20 provides the machinery presumption-of-conformity mechanism, supplemented by common specifications in defined circumstances. There is also a specific bridge to EU cybersecurity certification: where a cybersecurity certification scheme adopted under the Cybersecurity Act is appropriately referenced and covers the relevant requirements, it can support presumption of conformity for the protection-against-corruption/control-system requirements within the limits specified by the Regulation. That is very different from saying that any commercial _IEC 62443 certificate_ automatically proves Machinery Regulation compliance. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-026]

A significant current-status point is easily missed. _As of 3 October 2026, the Commission has still not published the first list of harmonised standards under Regulation (EU) 2023/1230._ The Commission states that the corresponding Implementing Decision is being prepared and is expected before the end of 2026. It is intended to carry over the vast majority of standards currently cited under Directive 2006/42/EC, while introducing limitations where existing standards do not fully address new or revised EHSRs of the Machinery Regulation. Meanwhile, the Directive-era list remains in force and was most recently amended by Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2015, adopted on 4 September and published in the Official Journal on 7 September 2026. That decision also provides for the repeal of Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1586 from **20 January 2027**, when Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 becomes applicable.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-027]

### EN 50742: the machinery-specific standard for protection against corruption

The new cyber-physical requirements of the Machinery Regulation are also generating a dedicated European standardisation response. **EN 50742, _Safety of machinery — Protection against corruption_, is being developed specifically to address the risks created when accidental or intentional corruption of hardware, software, data or communications can result in hazardous machinery behaviour.** It is therefore much closer to the legal logic of Annex III than a generic industrial cybersecurity standard.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-028]

The work is being developed within **CENELEC**, by **CLC/TC 44X — Safety of machinery: electrotechnical aspects**, with the detailed work assigned to **WG 2 — Protection against corruption (including safety-related cybersecurity aspects)**. This institutional placement is significant: the project sits within machinery electrotechnical safety standardisation rather than within a general information-security framework.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-en50742-committee]

Its intended relationship with Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 is explicit. The draft identifies **Annex III §1.1.9, _Protection against corruption_**, together with associated requirements in **§1.2.1(a)** and **§1.2.1(f)**, as the Machinery Regulation requirements it is intended to address. Its scope includes hardware components and interfaces—including interfaces to remote devices and control systems—as well as software and data where their corruption could influence machinery safety.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-en50742-scope]

This makes EN 50742 the natural intermediate layer between the Regulation and the more general industrial cybersecurity methods discussed later in this article. The Regulation defines the required **safety outcome**; EN 50742 is intended to translate the protection-against-corruption EHSRs into machinery-specific technical requirements and recommendations; IEC 62443 can then provide established cybersecurity concepts and controls—such as system integrity, identification and authentication, use control, restricted data flow and secure development—that may support implementation. The relationship should therefore not be read as **Machinery Regulation = IEC 62443**, but rather as a layered chain:

> **Machinery Regulation EHSR → EN 50742 machinery-specific interpretation → appropriate cybersecurity engineering controls**

The standard is being developed under the European Commission's **M/605 standardisation request**, issued to CEN and CENELEC in support of Regulation 2023/1230. This places the project within the formal process through which European standards can eventually become harmonised standards supporting the Regulation.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-en50742-m605]

As of **3 October 2026, however, EN 50742 has not yet been published as a final European Standard and has not been cited in the Official Journal under Regulation (EU) 2023/1230**. The project has progressed beyond the earlier public-enquiry draft and is now circulating as **FprEN 50742:2026** in the formal-approval phase. Even publication of the final EN will not, by itself, create a presumption of conformity: that legal effect arises only if and when its reference is published in the Official Journal under the Machinery Regulation.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-028]

## The machine is now partly software

The most consequential provisions are not hidden in a recital about cybersecurity. They are requirements in **Annex III**, meaning they become part of the safety case against which machinery conformity is assessed.

### Explicit digital requirements

The following table separates what the law actually says from the engineering response that may be reasonable.

| Legal provision | Regulatory requirement | Engineering meaning | Cybersecurity status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Article 3 — safety component** | A safety component can be physical or digital, including software, where the statutory conditions are met. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-029] | Safety software can itself fall inside the machinery product-compliance perimeter. | **Explicit** |
| **Article 3(16) — substantial modification** | Modification may be made by **physical or digital means** after market placement/putting into service. The remaining statutory safety/risk conditions must also be satisfied. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-030] | PLC logic, firmware, software configuration or remote-function changes cannot be dismissed merely because _nothing mechanical changed_. | **Explicit** |
| **Annex III §1.1.9 — connection** | Connection of another device, including through a remote device communicating with the machinery, must not lead to a hazardous situation. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-031] | Every control-capable communication path needs a safety consequence analysis. | **Explicit cyber-physical requirement** |
| **Annex III §1.1.9 — hardware** | Hardware transmitting signals/data relevant to access to compliance-critical software must be adequately protected against accidental or intentional corruption, with evidence of intervention collected where relevant. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-032] | Controller interfaces, engineering ports, gateways and update paths become part of the safety trust boundary. | **Explicit** |
| **Annex III §1.1.9 — software/data** | Software and data critical to EHSR compliance must be identified and adequately protected against accidental or intentional corruption. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-033] | Safety logic, configuration, safe-speed values, interlock mappings and integrity-critical datasets need protection. | **Explicit** |
| **Annex III §1.1.9 — software identity** | The machine must identify software installed on it that is necessary for safe operation and make that information accessible. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-034] | Software/firmware version inventory ceases to be merely an IT asset-management convenience. | **Explicit** |
| **Annex III §1.1.9 — intervention evidence** | Machinery must collect evidence of legitimate or illegitimate software intervention or modification of installed software/configuration. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-035] | Auditability/tamper evidence is required; a particular SIEM technology is not. | **Explicit logging/evidence obligation** |
| **Annex III §1.2.1(a)** | Control systems must, where appropriate to circumstances and risks, withstand intended/unintended external influences including **reasonably foreseeable malicious attempts from third parties leading to a hazardous situation**. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-036] | Threat modelling becomes relevant to the machinery safety case whenever an attacker can influence hazard controls. | **Explicit cybersecurity requirement** |
| **Annex III §1.2.1(d)** | Limits of safety functions are established through risk assessment; changes to settings/rules, including during learning, must not create hazardous situations. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-037] | Adaptive algorithms cannot be allowed to learn their way outside the validated safety envelope. | **Explicit; cyber controls may be one implementation** |
| **Annex III §1.2.1(f)** | Traceability of interventions and uploaded safety-software versions is to be enabled and retained for the prescribed period, including a five-year traceability requirement tied to safety-software uploads. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-038] | Version provenance and change history need to survive commissioning and service. | **Explicit** |
| **Annex III §1.2.1 — self-evolving systems** | Systems with fully or partially self-evolving behaviour/logic and varying autonomy must remain within defined task/movement boundaries and retain prescribed safety-decision information. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-039] | Runtime adaptation requires bounded authority and retrospective evidence. | **Explicit AI/autonomy requirement** |
| **Annex III §1.2.6** | Interruption, restoration or fluctuation of the power supply **or communication network connection** must not produce hazardous situations. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-040] | Loss-of-network, packet loss, reconnection and stale/replayed command conditions require safe-state analysis. | **Explicit digital-safety requirement** |
| **Annex IV technical documentation** | Safety-related source code or programming logic may have to be provided to a competent authority following a reasoned request where normal documentation is insufficient to demonstrate conformity. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-041] | _The PLC code is proprietary_ is not an absolute answer to a conformity investigation. | **Explicit compliance-evidence rule** |
| **Article 10 — instructions** | Manufacturers may use digital instructions subject to accessibility, availability and paper-safety-information conditions, particularly for non-professional users. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-042] | Documentation lifecycle and digital availability become product-compliance design questions. | **Digital modernisation, not cybersecurity per se** |

: Digital and cyber-relevant provisions of Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 and their engineering significance. {#tbl-digital-requirements}

A particularly important distinction emerges from §1.1.9. The Regulation does not prescribe a particular authentication protocol, firewall brand, cryptographic algorithm, secure-boot technology, MFA system, SBOM format or network topology. It states the **safety objective**: compliance-critical hardware, software and data must be protected against accidental and intentional corruption; connections must not create hazards; and interventions must leave evidence. Controls such as cryptographic firmware signing, role-based access, authenticated engineering sessions and configuration integrity checking are therefore **possible engineering means of satisfying the requirement**, not the literal requirement itself. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-043]

That distinction matters legally. A machine manufacturer should be able to produce a chain of reasoning of the form:

> **EHSR → identified cyber-physical hazard → security/safety requirement → chosen control → verification evidence**

rather than:

> **EHSR → _we use IEC 62443_ → assumed conformity.**

The latter skips the actual machinery risk assessment.

### Substantial modification by digital means

**Substantial modification is the other major digital change.** Article 3(16) expressly recognises modification _by physical or digital means_. But the term has a narrower legal meaning than _significant software change_. The modification must be made after market placement/putting into service, not be foreseen or planned by the original manufacturer, affect machinery safety by creating a new hazard or increasing an existing risk, and meet the further protective-measure conditions set out in the definition. Article 18 then provides that the natural or legal person carrying out such a substantial modification is considered a manufacturer for the purposes of the Regulation and assumes the corresponding obligations. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-044]

That produces very different answers for superficially similar digital changes:

| Change | Likely treatment under the Article 3(16) test |
|---|---|
| Manufacturer-planned cybersecurity firmware update, installed through the validated update process, with no change to the safety envelope | **Normally not substantial merely because it changes code.** It was foreseen and does not necessarily create/increase a hazard. Compliance and configuration evidence still matter. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-045] |
| HMI bug fix with no influence on safety functions or control authority | Usually outside the substantial-modification test, assuming the risk assessment confirms no safety impact. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-046] |
| Integrator modifies PLC/safety PLC logic so an interlocked guard can be opened during a new automatic mode and additional safeguarding or safety-control changes are required | Strong candidate for a substantial modification; Article 18 may make the integrator the manufacturer of the affected machinery. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-047] |
| Addition of permanent remote-control functionality not envisaged by the OEM, enabling machine motion from outside the original operator location | Not automatically substantial, but it may satisfy the test if it creates/increases risk and necessitates the statutory protective measures. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-048] |
| Cloud optimisation sends only recommendations that are validated and bounded by existing local safety/control limits | The presence of cloud software is not enough; the safety effect must be evaluated against Article 3(16). [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-049] |
| Cloud optimisation receives unrestricted write authority over speeds, trajectories or safety-relevant parameters | Much more likely to change the hazard/control model; whether it legally crosses the substantial-modification threshold still depends on the complete statutory test. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-050] |

: Examples illustrating how Article 3(16) may apply to digital modifications. {#tbl-substantial-modification-examples}

The practical lesson is that **_digital modification_ and _substantial modification_ are not synonyms**. Conversely, _we only changed software_ is no longer a viable categorical argument against the possibility of substantial modification. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-051]

## When a cyberattack becomes a machinery-safety event

The Regulation's cyber provisions are easier to interpret if the problem is modelled not as a catalogue of cybersecurity controls but as a **causal path from digital compromise to machinery hazard**. The crucial question is not simply whether a machine contains a vulnerability, but whether exploitation of that vulnerability can cross the machine's digital trust boundary, alter behaviour or control authority, and ultimately invalidate a safety assumption.

```{mermaid}

The resulting effects include altered commands, inhibited safety functions, corrupted sensing and unsafe behaviour under communication failure. Those control effects can create hazardous motion, excessive force or speed, defeated safeguards or unsafe operating states, which may expose people to harm. Annex III sections 1.1.9, 1.2.1 and 1.2.6 constrain different parts of this causal chain."
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {"theme": "neo", "look": "handDrawn", "layout": "elk"}}%%
```

The diagram separates three questions that are easy to collapse into a generic notion of _cybersecurity_:

1. There is the **attack path**: remote maintenance, an engineering workstation, a network interface, an update mechanism or a connected external service. These mechanisms are not hazardous merely because they are connected. They become relevant when they provide a route to a digital dependency on which safe machine behaviour relies.
2. There is the **digital dependency itself**: software, configuration, safety parameters, sensor data, communications or control authority. This is where Annex III §1.1.9 becomes particularly important. Its concern is not the existence of an exploitable vulnerability in the abstract, but the protection of hardware, software and data whose corruption can affect compliance with the applicable safety requirements.
3. Compromise must produce a **control-system consequence** before it becomes a machinery-safety event. The attacker may alter a command, inhibit a protective action, corrupt the machine's estimate of its physical state, change a validated operating limit or exploit the machine's response to communication loss or restoration. Those effects can then produce unexpected motion, excessive force or speed, defeated interlocks or another hazardous operating state.

This is where §1.2.1 adds a distinct requirement. Protection against corruption is not sufficient if the control architecture still permits a reasonably foreseeable malicious external influence to produce a hazardous situation. The Regulation therefore reaches beyond protection of individual digital assets and into the behaviour of the control system as a whole. Section 1.2.6 addresses a related but narrower causal path: interruption, restoration or fluctuation of a communication-network connection must itself not result in hazardous behaviour.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-052]

The important boundary is therefore:

> **cyber vulnerability ≠ machinery-safety non-conformity**

but, potentially,

> **cyber vulnerability → compromised safety-relevant dependency → unsafe control effect → hazardous machine state → possible failure of an applicable EHSR / machinery-safety non-conformity**

That distinction explains why the Regulation does not create a general-purpose OT cybersecurity regime. A compromise that exposes production data without affecting machinery behaviour may remain highly significant under the Cyber Resilience Act, NIS2 or the operator's own cybersecurity requirements, but it does not automatically become an Annex III machinery-safety failure. The Machinery Regulation becomes directly engaged when the digital compromise can alter the causal conditions under which the machine remains physically safe.

### Cyber-physical threat scenarios

This produces a useful threat model for industrial machinery.

| Threat scenario | Security consequence | Possible safety consequence | Principal Machinery Regulation hook |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stolen vendor credentials give an attacker engineering access to a PLC | Unauthorised logic/configuration modification | Unexpected motion or removal of safe sequencing | Annex III §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-053] |
| Safety PLC password/account compromised | Modification of safety logic or parameters | Guard bypass, incorrect safe-speed limit, defeated stop function | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| HMI compromised and command channel permits remote start | Control authority captured | Person exposed to unexpected start | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| Network injection changes VFD speed/torque command | Command integrity lost | Speed/force exceeds assumptions underlying risk reduction | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| OPC UA credentials permit writes to safety-relevant tags | Authorised protocol used by unauthorised actor | Safety envelope/setpoint altered | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| Manipulated sensor values | State estimation corrupted | Controller fails to detect person, obstruction or unsafe position | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| Malicious firmware update to drive/controller | Trusted execution base corrupted | STO/safe-motion or braking assumptions invalidated | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| Remote gateway compromise | New privileged path to internal controls | Any downstream unsafe control action enabled by the path | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| Network outage/reconnection creates stale or replayed command | Communications state loses integrity/availability | Unexpected restart, uncontrolled parameter change or inability to stop | §1.2.6 [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-054] |
| ML safety component poisoned or its parameters maliciously altered | Learned decision boundary changed | Safety decisions depart from validated limits | §1.2.1 and AI/ML provisions [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-055] |
| Production historian exfiltrated, with no ability to affect machine control | Confidentiality loss | No necessary physical safety effect | Possibly CRA/NIS2 issue; **not automatically an MR EHSR failure**. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-056] |

: Cyber-physical threat scenarios and the Machinery Regulation provisions they may implicate. {#tbl-cyber-physical-threat-scenarios}

This is why the expression **cyber-physical safety** is useful. It does not mean that safety and security have become identical. It means the independence assumption between the two domains is no longer defensible when security compromise can invalidate a safety assumption.

### Functional safety meets adversarial behaviour

Traditional machinery risk engineering remains indispensable. ISO 12100 specifies machinery risk assessment and risk reduction across relevant lifecycle phases; ISO 13849-1:2023 addresses the design and integration of safety-related parts of control systems, including software; IEC 62061:2021 addresses design, integration and validation of machinery safety-related control systems and is a machinery-sector implementation within the IEC 61508 framework. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-057]

What changes is the **failure model**. Performance Level or SIL reasoning can establish how a safety function tolerates defined random and systematic failures, but an adversary can intentionally select inputs, credentials, configuration pathways and timing to defeat assumptions shared across otherwise independent protection layers. A safety PLC with an excellent dangerous-failure probability does not solve the problem if an attacker can legitimately authenticate with a stolen engineering account and upload a hazardous configuration.

IEC itself now makes the relationship explicit in **IEC TS 63074:2023, _Safety of machinery — Security aspects related to functional safety of safety-related control systems._** The specification identifies IEC 62443 security threats and vulnerabilities that can lead to loss of the ability of a machinery safety-related control system to maintain safe operation and explicitly includes threat modelling in its scope. That is powerful evidence that functional safety and cybersecurity are distinct engineering disciplines whose risk models have to meet at the safety-related control system. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-058]

The risk-assessment implication can therefore be derived without overreading the Regulation:

1. Annex III §1.2.1 explicitly introduces reasonably foreseeable malicious third-party attempts into the control-system safety requirement. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-059]  
2. ISO 12100 requires identification and assessment of machinery hazards and risk reduction. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-060]  
3. IEC TS 63074 demonstrates that security threats/vulnerabilities can cause loss of machinery safety-control capability. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-061]  
4. Therefore, **where cyber compromise can defeat a risk-reduction measure or produce a hazardous state, the cyber pathway has to enter the machine safety analysis.**

That does not require calculating a SIL for _hacking_. It requires determining which cyber events can invalidate safety functions and ensuring that the machine architecture prevents, constrains or safely handles those events.

The most useful design question becomes:

> **What must an attacker be able to alter before this machine can hurt somebody?**

The answer identifies the machine's **safety-security trust boundary**: safety PLC logic, safety parameters, safe-motion configuration, firmware authenticity, interlock mapping, authorised modes, control ownership, sensor trust, update mechanisms and the communication paths capable of changing them.

## From connected machine to defensible architecture

### IEC 62443 as an engineering implementation framework

IEC 62443 is currently the strongest general engineering framework for translating that trust boundary into industrial cybersecurity architecture, but it must be used with the correct legal status. The IEC describes the 62443 series as addressing security of industrial automation and control systems throughout their lifecycle. IEC 62443-3-2 addresses system security risk assessment and zones/conduits; IEC 62443-3-3 provides system security requirements; IEC 62443-4-1 specifies a secure product-development lifecycle; and IEC 62443-4-2 specifies technical security requirements for IACS components. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-062]

**IEC 62443 is not made mandatory by Regulation (EU) 2023/1230**, nor, as of 3 October 2026, is there a Machinery Regulation harmonisation decision making the series a blanket presumption-of-conformity route for Annex III §§1.1.9 and 1.2.1. The first Machinery Regulation harmonised-standard list is still being prepared. EN 50742 is the more machinery-specific standardisation project explicitly entitled _Safety of machinery — Protection against corruption_; as of 3 October 2026 it has progressed to **FprEN 50742:2026** in the formal-approval phase, but has not yet been published as a final European Standard or cited in the Official Journal under the Machinery Regulation. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-063]

The correct relationship is therefore:

> **Machinery Regulation = required safety outcome** and **IEC 62443 = useful engineering mechanism for achieving and evidencing parts of that outcome**

not:

> **IEC 62443 certificate = automatic Machinery Regulation compliance.**

A practical mapping looks like this.

| Machinery concern | Useful IEC 62443 engineering layer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Identify malicious paths capable of changing machine state | **62443-3-2** | System-under-consideration analysis, zones/conduits and cybersecurity risk assessment. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-064] |
| Prevent unauthorised users/devices controlling machinery | **62443-3-3 / 4-2: Identification & Authentication Control, Use Control** | Authentication and authorisation support protection of safety-relevant access paths. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-065] |
| Prevent corruption of software/configuration | **System Integrity** in 3-3/4-2 plus 4-1 | Supports integrity, secure development, verification and controlled updates. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-066] |
| Restrict PLC/safety-controller exposure | **Restricted Data Flow; zones and conduits** | Limits paths from enterprise, cloud, vendor or HMI zones to control assets. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-067] |
| Generate evidence of intervention | **Timely Response to Events plus audit mechanisms** | Supports detection/event evidence; the MR itself establishes the safety-related evidence requirement. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-068] |
| Resist network/resource disruption | **Resource Availability** | Complements the MR §1.2.6 safe-behaviour requirement under network interruption. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-069] |
| Secure controller/product development | **62443-4-1** | Secure-development lifecycle, verification, defect and patch management. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-070] |
| Secure PLC/HMI/gateway components | **62443-4-2** | Component-level requirements for embedded, host, network and software components. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-071] |
| Secure OEM/integrator remote-service processes | **62443-2-4** | Security-program requirements for IACS service providers. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-072] |
| Operate and maintain the installed machine securely | **62443-2-1** | Asset-owner security management and lifecycle governance. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-073] |

: Mapping Machinery Regulation concerns to relevant IEC 62443 engineering layers. {#tbl-iec62443-mapping}

The seven 62443 foundational requirement families—identification and authentication control, use control, system integrity, data confidentiality, restricted data flow, timely response to events and resource availability—are useful, but their relevance to machinery safety is not symmetrical. **Integrity, authentication, use control, restricted data flow, event evidence and availability often have direct cyber-physical significance; confidentiality may be essential under other legislation yet have little machinery-safety significance unless loss of confidentiality enables or contributes to a hazardous attack.** [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-074]

### Reference architecture

A defensible connected-machine architecture should be derived from the **digital dependencies of the safety case**, not from operational convenience or inherited network topology. The objective is not simply to _segment the network_, but to ensure that **reachability, manageability and control authority remain distinct things**. A system may be reachable for monitoring without being reachable for administration; administrable without being able to program the controller; and able to exchange production data without being able to alter a safety limit.

That is why IEC 62443's zones-and-conduits model is useful here: it provides a structured way to separate systems according to function, trust level and required interaction, while Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 supplies the safety outcome that the architecture must protect.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-075]

A defensible connected-machine architecture can therefore be represented as follows:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-connected-machine-reference-architecture
%%| fig-cap: "Reference architecture for a connected industrial machine, separating enterprise and remote-service functions, plant OT integration, machine DMZ services, engineering access, machine control and safety functions."
%%| fig-alt: "The diagram shows a layered architecture. Vendor remote service reaches a default-off remote-access gateway using per-user MFA and VPN/TLS, then a jump host or session broker. Plant SCADA, MES and historians reach the machine through an OT firewall into a machine DMZ or industrial-edge zone. The machine DMZ contains mediated services such as protocol brokering, local historian, patch or update staging and telemetry export. It provides controlled access to the HMI and engineering zone. The engineering zone can reach the machine control zone through role-based, approved programming or operational sessions. The control zone has a tightly bounded interface to the safety zone. Logging, monitoring, backups and time synchronisation support the machine zones, and cloud analytics receives outbound telemetry only. There is no direct vendor, cloud or enterprise path to the control or safety zone."
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {"theme": "neo", "look": "handDrawn", "layout": "elk"}}%%

    end

    V -->|named user + MFA + VPN/TLS| R
    I -->|authorisation / approval context| R
    R -->|time-bounded session| J
    J -->|proxied remote maintenance| E

    P -->|application-specific OT flows| F

    C <--> |bounded control-safety interface| S

    C -->|status / alarms / production data| D
    D -->|outbound telemetry only| A

```

The diagram is intended to show **functional separation and authority separation**, not just layer-3 segmentation. It distinguishes six architectural roles:

1. **External and enterprise services.** These include vendor support, plant supervisory applications, cloud analytics, logging infrastructure and time synchronisation. They may be operationally necessary, but none of them should automatically inherit authority over machine execution or safety state.
2. **Plant OT boundary.** The OT firewall, remote-access gateway and jump or session-broker functions form the boundary through which external actors or plant-level systems reach the machine environment. This is where identity, approval, session initiation and high-level policy enforcement are anchored. In architectural terms, this boundary should convert generic connectivity into **explicitly mediated conduits**.
3. **Machine DMZ / industrial edge.** This zone is the integration and buffering layer between the machine and the plant or external world. It is the natural location for protocol mediation, local historians, edge brokers, update staging, telemetry export and similar boundary services. Its purpose is not merely to _sit between networks_, but to absorb functions that would otherwise create direct trust relationships with the machine-control environment.
4. **HMI / engineering zone.** This zone hosts the interfaces through which humans operate, diagnose, adjust or engineer the machine. It is a privileged zone and should be treated as such. It is frequently the practical bridge between business requirements and control logic, which makes it one of the most consequential trust boundaries in the machine.
5. **Machine control zone.** This is the execution plane of the machine: PLCs, robot controllers, CNCs, motion controllers and drives. It is the zone that turns logic and parameters into physical behaviour. It must not be treated as a generic OT subnet. From the standpoint of machinery safety, it contains assets whose corruption can directly change force, speed, movement, sequencing or actuation.
6. **Machine safety zone.** This contains the safety PLC, safe I/O, safe motion functions, interlocks and associated protective logic. It is not merely another controller subnet; it is the digital embodiment of protective functions on which the safety case relies. Its interface to the control zone should therefore be **tightly bounded, highly intentional and demonstrably justified**.

The architecture should then be read in terms of **conduits**, not only zones. The most important conduits are the following.

- **Remote-maintenance conduit:** vendor service → remote-access gateway → jump host/session broker → HMI/engineering zone. This conduit exists for troubleshooting and maintenance, not as a permanent, standing extension of the vendor network into the machine.
- **Plant-integration conduit:** plant SCADA/MES/historian → OT firewall → machine DMZ. This conduit should carry only those industrial data exchanges required for production, coordination or supervision. Its semantics matter: a read-only production-data flow is architecturally different from a recipe-write function, and both are different again from controller programming access.
- **Engineering conduit:** HMI/engineering zone → control zone. This is a high-consequence conduit because it often carries the authority to change logic, parameters and operating modes. For that reason, it should be mediated by role, session context and approval, not treated as an ordinary internal trust relationship.
- **Control–safety conduit:** control zone ↔ safety zone. This conduit must exist, but it should be deliberately narrow. Only the information and commands necessary for safe coordinated operation should cross it. Its design should support the principle that ordinary control or production functions cannot silently expand into safety authority.
- **Telemetry conduit:** machine DMZ → cloud analytics. This conduit should normally be outbound and scoped to telemetry or analytics data. The key architectural discipline is that a service justified by observation does not thereby acquire the right to command.
- **Evidence and support conduits:** machine zones → logging/monitoring/backup; time source → machine zones. These conduits support traceability, recovery and temporal coherence. They matter directly because the Regulation requires evidence of intervention and traceability of safety-relevant software changes, while distributed troubleshooting and forensics become unreliable without trustworthy time alignment.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-076]

The architectural principle that follows is simple but far-reaching:

> **Connectivity should not automatically confer control authority.**

An OPC UA session used to read production counts does not inherently need to write a speed limit. A cloud analytics service used for predictive maintenance does not inherently need controller-programming rights. An OEM maintenance tunnel does not inherently need permanent reachability to a safety PLC. A MES recipe service does not inherently need authority to overwrite the parameters that delimit a validated safe-motion function.

That is **least privilege applied to physical causality**. The relevant question is not only _what access does this system need?_ but **_what hazardous physical effect could this system produce if its authority were abused or its integrity lost?_** This is the point at which enterprise-architecture thinking and machinery-safety analysis meet: authority has to be modelled not just by user role or application function, but by the physical consequences that the granted capability can trigger.

This also means that the reference architecture should separate at least four kinds of authority:

- **observe**: read data, alarms, states, logs or telemetry;
- **operate**: initiate normal production commands within the validated operating envelope;
- **configure**: change parameters, recipes or settings that influence machine behaviour;
- **engineer**: alter logic, firmware, safety functions or the configuration baseline itself.

These should not be conflated. Many connected systems need observation. Fewer need operation. Very few should be able to configure behaviour, and fewer still should be able to engineer the machine. Where those capabilities are combined, the safety case should explain why.

The safety zone should therefore have the **narrowest trust boundary in the entire architecture**. Depending on the machine and the risk assessment, appropriate engineering measures may include separate engineering roles, local enable conditions for especially sensitive actions, validated parameter ranges, cryptographically protected configuration where supported, signed or hashed baselines, authenticated software loading, independently enforced safe-motion constraints, strict change traceability and monitored access. None of these mechanisms is prescribed verbatim by Annex III. Their justification is architectural: they reduce the number of paths by which corruption or malicious influence can invalidate a protective function.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-076]

It is equally important to say what the reference architecture normally **excludes**:

- no direct Internet path to PLCs, robot controllers, drives or safety controllers;
- no direct cloud-to-controller write path justified merely by analytical convenience;
- no permanent vendor tunnel that bypasses plant approval and session control;
- no flat trust relationship between HMI/engineering systems and safety logic;
- no assumption that _internal OT_ is sufficiently trusted to dispense with attribution, role separation or evidence of change;
- no uncontrolled path by which enterprise systems can acquire machine-control authority.

This is why the architecture should be understood as an **authority architecture**, not just a network diagram. The legal driver is still the Machinery Regulation's requirement that connections, corruption and malicious external influence must not lead to hazardous situations. The engineering task is to translate that into zones, conduits, identities, roles, approval paths, software integrity controls, evidence generation and recovery design. In that sense, the diagram is not merely an illustration of segmentation. It is a model of how to preserve the assumptions under which the machine remains physically safe.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-075]

### Remote access is remote authority

**Remote access deserves special treatment because it collapses geography without reducing authority.** An engineer thousands of kilometres away can, depending on implementation, possess the same logical privileges as a person connected locally to an engineering port. In some architectures, the remote path can be even more consequential because it traverses several independently administered systems—vendor identity infrastructure, VPN concentrators, cloud brokers, jump hosts, engineering workstations and machine controllers—before reaching the asset that can produce physical motion.

For machinery safety, the relevant architectural question is therefore not simply whether remote access is encrypted. It is:

> **What machine authority becomes available when the remote session succeeds?**

A VPN may provide excellent cryptographic protection while still exposing an unnecessarily broad control surface. MFA may reduce credential theft without limiting what an authenticated engineer can change. A jump host may create an auditable choke point while still permitting unrestricted PLC or safety-PLC programming. These controls are important, but their safety value depends on the **authority exposed beyond them**.

Annex III does not prescribe *MFA*, *PAM*, *jump hosts* or a particular VPN architecture. It establishes the safety outcome: connected or remote paths must not create hazardous situations, compliance-critical software and data must be protected against corruption, and relevant control systems must withstand reasonably foreseeable malicious attempts capable of producing hazards.[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-077]

Remote maintenance should therefore be modelled as a **privileged control conduit with a lifecycle**, rather than as a permanent network connection.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-remote-maintenance-authority-lifecycle
%%| fig-cap: "Reference control model for privileged remote maintenance, separating request, authorisation, connectivity, session authority, safety-sensitive change control and post-session evidence."
%%| fig-alt: "The diagram shows remote maintenance beginning from a default-deny state. A named vendor engineer authenticates through MFA, after which the plant or machine owner authorises a specific request. A temporary conduit is established through a plant-controlled remote-access gateway and jump or session broker. The session is assigned an authority class such as observe, operate, configure or engineer. Engineering or safety-sensitive changes require additional approval and, where justified by the risk assessment, a local enabling condition. Activity is monitored and logged. At the end of the session, the connection and temporary privileges are revoked, configuration changes are reconciled against the approved baseline and evidence is retained."
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {"theme": "neo", "look": "handDrawn", "layout": "elk"}}%%
flowchart TD

    A[Default deny<br/>no active remote path]

    subgraph ID["Identity and request"]
        B[Named engineer<br/>individual identity]
        C[MFA / credential validation]
        D[Maintenance request<br/>asset + purpose + scope]
    end

    subgraph AUTH["Plant authorisation"]
        E[Owner / operator approval]
        F[Maintenance window<br/>time limitation]
        G[Requested authority class]
    end

    subgraph PATH["Controlled remote conduit"]
        H[Remote Access Gateway<br/>plant controlled]
        I[Jump Host / Session Broker]
        J[Protocol / destination restriction]
    end

    subgraph AUTHORITY["Granted machine authority"]
        K1[Observe<br/>read-only]
        K2[Operate<br/>validated commands]
        K3[Configure<br/>parameters / recipes]
        K4[Engineer<br/>logic / firmware / safety]
    end

    subgraph SAFETY["Safety-sensitive change gate"]
        L[Change request / approved task]
        M[Elevated privilege]
        N[Local enabling condition<br/>where risk justifies]
        O[PLC / safety PLC / drive<br/>programming or configuration]
    end

    subgraph EVIDENCE["Monitoring and closure"]
        P[Session monitoring<br/>user + target + actions]
        Q[Configuration / software<br/>change evidence]
        R[Session termination]
        S[Automatic privilege<br/>and tunnel revocation]
        T[Baseline reconciliation<br/>and retained evidence]
    end

    A --> B
    B --> C
    C --> D
    D --> E
    E --> F
    F --> G
    G --> H
    H --> I
    I --> J

    J --> K1
    J --> K2
    J --> K3
    J --> K4

    K1 --> P
    K2 --> P
    K3 --> P
    K4 --> L

    M --> N
    N --> O
    O --> P
```
